analysis.one_liner: Repeals dozens of corporate tax breaks and requires market prices for federal lands and resources sold to companies.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a single sponsor with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to six House committees and more than a dozen subcommittees, and it died without a hearing or a vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have wiped out roughly two dozen tax breaks used mainly by oil and gas companies, hardrock miners, timber growers, farm businesses, insurers, magazine publishers, and multinational corporations. It would also have ended the practice of selling or leasing federal timber, minerals, water, grazing land, and hydroelectric power to companies for less than fair market value, and imposed an 8 percent royalty and annual fees on hardrock mining on public land. Money the government currently forgoes would have gone to the Treasury as deficit reduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would stop footing the bill for tax breaks and below-cost sales of public assets, and companies that compete without subsidies, which would face rivals no longer supported by the tax code. The abandoned-mine reclamation fund would direct mining royalties toward cleaning up damaged land and water.

how_it_helps.text: Ends the deduction for oil and gas drilling and mining exploration costs and repeals percentage depletion, which lets mineral producers deduct a fixed share of income regardless of actual costs.
Repeals the enhanced oil recovery credit, the credit for fuel from nonconventional sources, tax benefits for alcohol fuels, and the deduction for tertiary injectants.
Requires that timber, minerals, forage, federally owned water, and hydroelectric energy from federal facilities never be sold, leased, or disposed of for less than fair market value.

Imposes an 8 percent royalty on production from hardrock mining claims on federal land, a $100 annual claim maintenance fee, and a separate severance excise tax, with royalties and taxes credited to a new abandoned-mine reclamation fund.

Sets livestock grazing fees at fair market value, prohibits below-cost timber sales from national forests, and requires public-lands oil and gas rentals and communications-site permits to be priced at fair market value.

Ends special tax treatment for Blue Cross and Blue Shield organizations, small life insurance companies, and small property and casualty insurers, and repeals the tax exclusion for foreign sales corporations and the deferral of controlled foreign corporation income, taxing more corporate profit earned overseas.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, hardrock mining companies, timber growers, ranchers, farm businesses, insurers, magazine publishers, and multinational corporations would lose tax breaks or pay market prices for federal resources. U.S. citizens living abroad would also lose a personal income exclusion under the bill's text.

drawbacks.text: The bill would end the foreign earned income exclusion, raising taxes on individual U.S. citizens living abroad — a personal tax break, not a corporate subsidy.

The farm provisions — repealing cash-method accounting, fertilizer and soil-and-water conservation deductions, and the livestock feed assistance program — would raise costs for small family farms as well as large agribusiness.

Repealing the credits and deductions for electric and clean-fuel vehicles, refueling property, and alcohol fuels would eliminate the tax-code incentives then available for alternative-fuel vehicles and fuels.
Higher royalties, fees, and grazing and rental charges on public-land users could be passed through to consumers in prices for food, minerals, and wood products.
The bill never received a hearing or markup in any committee, so its revenue estimates and economic effects were never tested or revised.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — ending tax breaks for extraction industries and charging market value for public assets — would shift costs from taxpayers to the industries that use them, and the abandoned-mine fund would put mining royalties to visible public use. But the bill was written broadly and bluntly: it sweeps in provisions that hit individuals abroad and family farms alongside genuine corporate giveaways, and because no committee ever examined it, there were no published cost estimates or any chance to separate the well-targeted provisions from the problematic ones.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees and then split among more than a dozen subcommittees, and no committee ever held a hearing or brought it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the Corporate Welfare Elimination Act of 2001 on May 17, 2001, as the bill's only sponsor.

The bill was referred to the Ways and Means, Resources, Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Budget Committees, and within two weeks further referred to at least fifteen subcommittees across those panels.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil, gas, mining, timber, ranching, farm, insurance, publishing, and multinational interests that the bill targeted kept their tax breaks and their below-market access to federal land and resources, and taxpayers kept paying for them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil, gas, mining, and farm subsidy recipients

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee

against.what_they_did: Received the tax-title referral and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.what_they_did: Received referral of the mining, grazing, and timber provisions and referred them to four subcommittees without further action.

against.what_they_did: Received referral of the farm subsidy and accounting provisions and referred them to four subcommittees without further action.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken, the sole sponsor was a Democrat, and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so support and opposition were never measured.

industries.note: The bill repeals intangible drilling cost expensing, percentage depletion, the enhanced oil recovery credit, tertiary injectant deductions, and below-market public-lands lease rentals — a bundle of long-standing oil and gas tax preferences paid for by other taxpayers.

The bill would impose the first 8 percent royalty, a $100 annual claim fee, and a severance tax on gold and other hardrock mining on federal land, ending the 1872-era practice of removing minerals with no royalty while leaving the public to reclaim abandoned mines.

It bans below-cost timber sales from national forests and repeals the reforestation credit and timber expensing, ending sales in which the Forest Service lost money on logging that private buyers purchased cheaply.

industries.industry: Livestock ranchers grazing on public land
industries.note: Grazing fees would rise to fair market value under a set formula; today federal grazing rates run well below private-land rates, a subsidy to ranchers paid in degraded public rangeland and forgone revenue.

The bill repeals cash-method accounting, fertilizer and conservation deductions, farm-debt and cost-sharing exclusions, and the livestock feed assistance program; large agribusiness loses its tax preferences, but small family farms also lose benefits that help them stay afloat.

It repeals the special tax treatment of Blue Cross and Blue Shield organizations, the small life insurance company deduction, and the alternative tax for small property and casualty insurers, removing carve-outs other taxpayers effectively subsidize.

The bill repeals the foreign sales corporation exclusion and deferral of controlled foreign corporation income, subjecting more foreign-earned corporate profit to U.S. tax instead of allowing it to sit offshore untaxed.
It repeals the special deduction for magazine circulation spending and the tax rules for returned magazines, paperbacks, and records — preferences unique to the publishing industry.
It ends the tax deferral under the Merchant Marine Capital Construction Fund, a benefit available to few other industries.
